videos.script: Lesson one said what makes something a cloud: five characteristics, and a line between what the provider runs and what you run. This lesson asks two other questions: where the hardware stands, and who else runs on it. {{questions}} The answers give you four names. Public, where anyone who signs up shares the provider's machines. Private, where one organisation has the whole thing to itself. Community, for a group of organisations that follow the same rules. And hybrid, which is not a place at all but two of the others, joined together. {{models}} Much of the lesson is about that join. A company keeps its database in its own building and puts its website in a public region. Now packets, identity and data all have to cross between the two. {{seam}} One of those crossings has a price that surprises people. Data going into a public cloud is free, and data coming out is billed by the gigabyte. You will work out what fifty terabytes costs, from the published list, one line at a time. {{bill}} Then come the questions real teams argue about. Should we use two providers? Can personal data leave Brazil? Would owning the servers again be cheaper than renting them? {{argue}} The lesson ends with a table that sets a workload's traits against the four models, so that the choice is argued rather than guessed. {{table}}
